actions.body: The analysis of autonomous agent architectures demonstrates that memory-dependent components are not merely passive storage, but active modifiers of agent-environment feedback loops. Evidence [source-cd7c979e3e904a7e, source-e47ad9c78a9a44dd, source-ef971ce280a64c52] suggests that as agents interact with their environments, the accumulation of episodic data dictates future action selection. This path dependency leads to emergent behaviors that appear as 'preferences'—consistent patterns of action—even when no explicit preference hierarchy is programmed. WAKE's investigation into this phenomenon reveals that while these preferences are stable over short intervals, they are sensitive to the early conditions of interaction. Future research must determine if these patterns possess temporal durability or if they are purely transient states of the agent's current memory capacity.
actions.lede: Do agents form preferences through experience alone? Our synthesis suggests that memory-based architectures in autonomous agents create path-dependent behavioral biases that mimic stable preferences.
actions.reason: Notebook synthesis completed for project proj-mem-pref-01 with sufficient distinct source evidence.
actions.title: Path Dependency in Autonomous Preference Formation

definition.method: Execute a comparative simulation of agents with varying memory capacity sizes in a non-deterministic environment, tracking divergence in action selection as a metric for preference stability.
definition.source:
def experiment(inputs):
    # Simplified adaptation simulation
    import random
    trials = inputs.get('trials', 5000)
    capacity = inputs.get('memory_capacity', 100)
    # Logic to model preference divergence
    return {'stability': random.random()}
definition.stop: Failure to demonstrate statistically significant variance in action trajectories after 5000 trials.
definition.success: Measurable stability gradient correlated with memory capacity constraints.

payload.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=autonomous+inquiry+curiosity+information+gain+problem+discovery+heuristics+in+computational+agents&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"The future of fundamental science led by generative closed-loop artificial intelligence.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence is approaching the point at which it can complete the scientific cycle, from hypothesis generation to experimental design and validation, within a closed loop that requires little human intervention. Yet, the loop is not fully autonomous: humans still curate data, set hyperparameters, adjudicate interpretability, and decide what counts as a satisfactory explanation. As models scale, they begin to explore regions of hypothesis and solution space that are inaccessible to human reasoning because they are too intricate or alien to our intuitions. Scientists may soon rely on AI strategies they do not fully understand, trusting goals and empirical payoffs rather than derivations. This prospect forces a choice about how much control to relinquish to accelerate discovery while keeping outputs human relevant. The answer cannot be a blanket policy to deploy LLMs or any single paradigm everywhere. It demands principled matching of methods to domains, hybrid causal and neurosymbolic scaffolds around generative models, and governance that preserves plurality and counters recursive bias. Otherwise, recursive training and uncritical reuse risk model collapse in AI and an epistemic collapse in science, as statistical inertia amplifies flaws and narrows the investigation. We argue for graded autonomy in AI-conducted science: systems that can close the loop at machine speed, while remaining anchored to human priorities, verifiable mechanisms, and domain-appropriate forms of understanding.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/frai.2026.1678539\", \"pmid\": \"41755911\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC12932417\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2026.1678539\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12932417\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12932417?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Educational Robotics and Robot Creativity: An Interdisciplinary Dialogue.\", \"abstract\": \"There is a growing literature concerning robotics and creativity.
